headline: Moga Stubble Fire Update and Bathinda Air Quality Forecast
briefing: On October 31, 2025, Moga recorded 11 fire detections with a total fire radiative power of 54.5 MW. This reflects a 285.0% change compared to its 7-day mean of 2.9, placing Moga rank 8 in Punjab out of 273 total detections across the state. In the 2024 season, Moga logged 562 detections [K103]. Satellite counts serve as a lower bound since overpasses miss brief fires [K026]. At the nearest monitored city, Bathinda, today's PM2.5 level is 105.6. The next-day PM2.5 forecast predicts a median of 102.3, with an 80% uncertainty band spanning from a p10 of 61.8 to a p90 of 131.2. Wind at Bathinda blows from the NNW (331.0 degrees) at 6.8 km/h. Upwind fire pressure reaches 715.8, with Outside Punjab contributing 64.1%, Tarn Taran 13.0%, and Ferozepur 5.9%. Upwind fires provide regional context rather than proof of direct PM2.5 impact.

The busiest day was 2024-11-18, with 119 detections.

Compared with the previous season: -75% compared with 2023 (2,286 detections).

results.title: How satellite fire detection (VIIRS, NASA FIRMS) works and what it misses
results.text:
# How satellite fire detection works

NASA FIRMS distributes active fire detections from the VIIRS instrument on the Suomi NPP (S-NPP) satellite. This project uses only S-NPP, so every year is seen by the same sensor. The VIIRS active fire product has a pixel size of about 375 m. Each detection is a pixel that looks hotter than its surroundings in the thermal infrared bands. Each record has a date, a time (UTC), a position, a fire radiative power (FRP, in megawatts) and a confidence class of low, nominal or high. We drop the low-confidence records.

results.title: How satellite fire detection (VIIRS, NASA FIRMS) works and what it misses
results.text:
# Why fires are missed

- **Overpass timing.** S-NPP passes over a place about twice a day, at roughly 01:30 and 13:30 local solar time. A fire that starts and burns out between two passes is never seen.
- **Cloud and thick smoke.** The sensor cannot see through thick cloud, so fires under it are missed.
- **Small or weak fires.** Small, short or low-intensity burns can fall below the detection threshold of a 375 m pixel.

So a detection count is a lower bound that moves with the weather and the overpass timing. It is not a census of fires.
